name: Hairstyle maxxing

lead: Hairstyle maxxing is picking a haircut and styling to suit your face shape, forehead size, head shape and hair type. The payoff is visible right after the cut: hair adds volume and texture, frames the face and hairline, and changes how much forehead and eye area shows.

Research in person perception treats hairstyle, clothing and makeup as part of first impressions, and a 2023 review argues dress, including hairstyle, belongs in models of how people judge one another. No trial has tested face-shape-matching rules as such.

paras: People bring reference photos to a barber or stylist and adjust length, volume, fringe and parting to their face and growth pattern. Many add styling products, and some use chemical straightening or waving. Forums are full of photo threads asking for hairstyle suggestions.
Haircuts are reversible and grow out. Dermatology reviews report that tight, tension-heavy styles can cause traction alopecia, and chemical straightening or waving carries its own review literature.

angle.text: Users pick a cut and styling to suit face shape, forehead size and hair type, and the change is visible as soon as the haircut is done. Research shows hair shapes first impressions.

lead: Hairstyle maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of choosing hair length, cut and styling to improve overall appearance, particularly by matching the style to face shape, forehead size, hair type and hair density. Hair is the most changeable thing on the head: a cut can be redone within weeks, which is why forum members rank it among the cheapest and fastest appearance variables. Rating and advice threads on looksmax.org are full of requests for hairstyle suggestions accompanied by front and side photos. [1][2]

Proponents say hair adds volume and texture around the face, can alter perceived forehead height and face width, and can frame the eyes; some call this effect the 'hair halo' and say that even very highly rated faces change noticeably between hairstyles. [3] A hairstyle is any arrangement of hair, and historically styles have signalled age, status, religion and identity. [4] A 2023 review in Personality and Social Psychology Review argues that dress, including hairstyle, makeup and accessories, influences first impressions and belongs in models of person perception. [5]

The topic overlaps with barbering and fades, buzz cuts for men with receding hairlines, texturising and straightening treatments, and hair restoration. [6][7][8][9][10] No published trial has tested whether a given cut flatters a given face shape, but the neighbouring literatures on first impressions, face recognition and scalp health are substantial. [5][11][12]

Hair restoration, minoxidil and finasteride, beard grooming, straightening and waving [6][9]

Braided hair on figurines about 30,000 years old [4]

paras: Hairstyle maxxing covers cut, length, fringe, parting, texture and styling products. Encyclopedia coverage of hairstyling lists defining factors including hair type, face and head shape, body proportions, self-image and the stylist's judgment. [4]

Hairstyles have long carried social meaning: the oldest known depiction of hair styling is braiding on a roughly 30,000-year-old figurine, and styles have marked marital status, class, religion and subculture across eras. [4] Elites historically used elaborate styles to show they did not need to work, while middle-class styles tend to look healthy and natural. [4]

Wikipedia notes that in 1624 Louis XIII of France is reported to have pioneered the male wig after balding early, that Charles II brought periwigs to England in 1660, and that the Bedford Crop, a short cut associated with the Duke of Bedford, was a protest against the 1795 tax on hair powder. [4] Short back and sides is traced to Roman legionaries, returned in the Regency era after the powder tax, and by 1910 had become the norm for professional men. [13]

In the 1920s and 1930s film stars such as Rudolph Valentino and Douglas Fairbanks Jr. popularised short pomaded styles, and crew cuts appeared around the Second World War. [4] Long natural hair spread through the counterculture of the 1960s and 1970s, while the Afro became a political statement in the 1960s. [4] Grokipedia, citing trend roundups, says that after 2021 men increasingly chose slicked-back looks and that medium-length textured styles have grown in popularity relative to rigid fades. [14]

Barbering itself is ancient: Wikipedia says the first barbering services date to around 5000 BC in Egypt, barbering reached Rome in 296 BC, and medieval barbers also worked as surgeons. In the United States many states license barbers, with training requirements ranging from about 800 to 2,000 hours. [7]

A taper graduates hair length from the top of the head down to the lower edge of the back and sides; the short taper, also called a fade, uses a coarse clipper from the lower hairline and a finer clipper above the ear, with the lines blended. [13] Buzz, brush, crew and flattop cuts are listed as short clipper variants, and Wikipedia says buzz cuts suit men with thinning or receding hairlines and men who want a low-maintenance style. [8]

Stylists often cut straight hair wet and curly textures dry, and use clippers, scissors, razors and thinning shears to shape and blend layers. Gels, mousses, waxes and sprays are standard products, and excessive heat from curling or flat irons (which can reach roughly 150 to 230 degrees Celsius) can damage hair. [4]

Texture-changing treatments include heat straightening, keratin and Japanese thermal reconditioning, relaxers based on sodium hydroxide, and permanent waves. Hot combs were on sale in Europe and America by the 1870s, and Madam C. J. Walker popularised the straightening comb in the early 1900s. [9] Dermatology reviews describe the processes and what dermatologists should know about each. [15][16]

Many looksmaxxers discuss hairstyle in relation to male pattern hair loss, which Wikipedia says affects about half of men by age 50, and which is graded on the Hamilton-Norwood scale. [6] A looksmax.org thread title shows the topic is treated on its own, with a thread on hairstyles for men with hair loss (Norwoods). [17]

Wikipedia's article on male pattern baldness lists styling remaining hair, shaving the head and cosmetic scalp tattoos that mimic a short buzz cut among ways to conceal thinning, alongside treatments such as finasteride, minoxidil and low-level laser therapy and surgical transplantation. [6] Hair transplantation has a recorded history reaching back to 1897 (Menahem Hodara), with Norman Orentreich showing in the late 1950s that transplanted hair keeps its donor properties, strip and follicular-unit extraction methods developed later, and robotic systems from NeoGraft and ARTAS receiving FDA clearance in 2009 to 2011. [10]
Men typically find hair loss moderately stressful and report reduced body-image satisfaction, but Wikipedia says most cope well and keep their sense of identity. [6]

sections.h: Face shape and hair in looksmaxxing
paras: Forum advice commonly pairs a haircut with a face feature. One poster with a tall skull says a fringe makes the face appear wider and that showing the forehead seems to bring harmony; a reply suggests long fluffy hair that flares out and covers part of the forehead while leaving the eye area visible. [2] Other threads ask for styles for a long face and big forehead. [18]

One poster argues that hair adds volume and texture to the face, that a good haircut can 'ascend' the face and hide major flaws, and that many TikTok personalities 'ride on their hair halo'; replies say the face matters above all and that a haircut will not rescue features below a certain level. [3] The claim that a cut should be matched to face shape is common in barbering and fashion guides generally; encyclopedia coverage lists face and head shape among the defining factors of a hairstyle. [4]

A 2023 review in Personality and Social Psychology Review states that clothing, hairstyle, makeup and accessories influence first impressions, and proposes that perceivers use dress to infer social category, cognitive state, status and aesthetics. [5] The review is a theoretical proposal and does not test face-shape-matching rules.

Face-recognition experiments report that hairstyle is an external feature whose importance falls as a face becomes familiar, with internal features such as eyes, nose and mouth becoming more salient. [11] Within-person variation, including hairstyle changes, has been studied in the context of face learning. [19] Grokipedia states that preferences for particular hair lengths and styles correlate with perceived attractiveness and status across cultures, and cites a paper titled 'Hairstyle as an adaptive means of displaying phenotypic quality', though it gives no authors or date. [14]

Traction alopecia is hair loss from chronic pulling. Wikipedia lists tight ponytails, braids, weaves, extensions, dreadlocks and some headgear as causes, and says it is reported most often in African-American women, and also in ballerinas and Sikh men and women; management centres on stopping the traction. [20] A review reports that traction alopecia affects up to 32 percent of women and 22 percent of high school girls with Afro-textured hair, with risk rising with tight or combined styles. [12] A 2016 American Academy of Dermatology study cited by Wikipedia found that tight braids can cause traction alopecia and recommended looser styles and shorter braid durations. [4]

A study of 874 African adults in Cape Town examined the relation between hairdressing practices and scalp disease. [21] A further study examined marginal traction alopecia in African girls and women. [22]

Chemical relaxers can cause scalp irritation, hair loss, chemical burns and breakage, and Wikipedia reports that NIH-funded research has linked chemicals in some relaxers to breast and uterine cancers, including a 2017 study in which relaxer users were nearly twice as likely to develop breast cancer. Keratin treatments emit gases and are not recommended during pregnancy. [9] Hair transplantation commonly causes temporary 'shock loss' of existing hair. [10]

Threads on looksmax.org include hairstyle-name requests and advice on styles for long faces or tall foreheads. [2][18] One poster reports that comments on his hair changed as his body fat rose, which he reads as hair only looking good on an already good-looking face. [1]
In looksmaxxing, hair is usually treated as one layer in a stack with skincare, leanness and grooming, rather than as an independent fix. [1][3]

No studies found on matching hairstyle to face shape as an appearance intervention. Related research covers hairstyle in person perception and face recognition [5][11], and the scalp-health literature on traction and chemical styling [12][15][16].

lore.intro: Members treat hair as one of the highest-leverage and cheapest appearance variables, and the topic is a staple of rating and advice threads. [1][2][3]

claims.claim: A good haircut can frame the face and hide flaws (the 'hair halo').
Hairstyle only helps if the underlying face is already attractive.
Showing the forehead or adding a fringe changes how harmonious the face looks.
Hairstyle choice should depend on face shape.
A short cut or buzz cut is a good answer to a receding hairline.
Tight styles and chemical processing are harmless to the hair.
